Title: Re-Thinking Teaching (RTT) Workshop, AKU Karachi
NewsSubTitle: RTT held in Karachi on 26th to 29th September 2017
NewsSummary: The RTT held in Karachi on 26th to 29th September 2017 was similar to the one held earlier in Nairobi, Kenya on July 25th to July 29th 2017.
NewsContent:
Research over the past few decades has had profound implications on teaching. It is imperative that this research be brought into the classrooms of progressive universities like AKU. However, unpacking previous learning and making a paradigm shift from a content-centered approach to a learning-centered approach is difficult. This is what Re-thinking Teaching workshop is all about. It is a four day workshop for faculty to examine and develop their thinking about the course design process and their teaching practice. 

The RTT held in Karachi on 26th to 29th September 2017 was similar to the one held earlier in Nairobi, Kenya on July 25th to July 29th 2017. Geraldine Van Gyn, an Emeritus Professor, University of Victoria, British Columbia, Canada and staff from the Teaching and Learning Network facilitated the four day workshop. The workshop in Karachi brought together teaching faculty from IED, DED, SONAM and Medical College. There was need to train faculty to re-design their courses. Interactive small and large group sessions, and peer learning provided opportunities for participants to develop principles of curriculum framework including concepts, learning outcomes, active learning strategies and assessment that can be used across multiple disciplines. Participants were able to link teaching directly to student learning through a course design process that involved:

  • Conceptualizing the course through the development of a concept map
  • Drafting of learning outcomes for the course
  • Determining suitable assessment approaches
  • Selecting appropriate instructional strategies aligned with the learning outcomes

On the last day of the workshop, each participant show-cased plans for their re-designed course in a 90 second presentation followed by an interactive session of feedback and discussion. At the end of the workshop, most agreed that while their curricula may be masterpieces, they were also "work in progress"! 

The feedback from participants was not only positive but many said it had completely changed their thinking on how to design their courses. One participant went as far as to say that while he thought his course design was perfect this workshop had opened his eyes to its imperfections! Most participants said that the workshop should be made mandatory for all teaching faculty.
